newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya opposition splits further ahead of polls.
newsitem.headline: Kenya opposition splits further ahead of polls.

text.p: Kenya's opposition movement appeared in further disarray on Friday after a key politician in the FORD-Asili party said it had replaced party chairman and presidential candidate Kenneth Matiba.
FORD-Asili Secretary-General Martin Shikuku said party vice-chairman George Nthenge had been appointed chairman after Matiba failed to attend an internal disciplinary meeting.
Matiba was accused of indiscipline and gross misconduct. He has rejected such allegations and branded Shikuku "a spoiler".
George Nyanja, a member of parliament and Matiba ally, said the move to replace Matiba was illegal and was part of a plot to bar Matiba from contesting the presidency later this year.
"This is a major plot to stop Matiba from contesting the presidency. It is illegal," Nyanja told Reuters.

Matiba ranked second behind President Daniel arap Moi in landmark multi-party elections held in December 1992. Moi has pledged that parliamentary and presidential elections will be held sometime this year.
Under Kenyan laws, a presidential candidate must be nominated by a party. No independents are allowed.
The FORD-Asili split follows a split in the main opposition FORD-Kenya party headed by Michael Kijana Wamalwa.

Radical opposition politician Raila Odinga left the FORD-Kenya party his father Jaramogi Oginga Odinga helped found on New Year's eve to join the National Development Party of Kenya that has now made him a presidential candidate.
FORD-Asili and FORD-Kenya are themselves a result of a split in the Forum for the Restoration of Democracy (FORD) that had threatened to sweep Moi and his KANU party from power in 1992.
Moderate opposition members of parliament are urging their colleagues to rally behind Charity Kaluki Ngilu as a compromise presidential candidate to avoid further splits on tribal lines.
Kenyan opposition leaders agree on broad issues such as a need for constitutional reforms before the elections but appear to differ on almost everything else.
